_note: General guidance only. Recycling rules differ by city and country, so always check local rules.

battery.bin: Special battery collection point (not any household bin)
prepare: Cover the terminals of lithium or button batteries with tape.
Store used batteries in a dry, non-metal container until drop-off.
battery.dispose: Take to a battery drop-off box in a supermarket, electronics shop, or a hazardous-waste collection point.
avoid: Do not put batteries in general waste or recycling bins.
Do not crush, burn, or open them.
battery.tip: Damaged lithium batteries can start fires in bins and collection trucks.
battery.environment: Batteries contain metals that can leak into soil and water if landfilled, and the metals inside can be recovered when recycled properly.

biological.bin: Food / organic waste bin or home compost
prepare: Remove any plastic, foil, or packaging.
Drain excess liquid.
biological.dispose: Place in the food-waste or compost bin. If your area has no collection, home composting works for most fruit, vegetable, and garden waste.
avoid: Do not put organic waste in the recycling bin; it contaminates paper and cardboard.
biological.tip: Cooked food, meat, and dairy usually suit municipal food-waste collection but not simple home compost heaps.
biological.environment: Food waste in landfill breaks down without oxygen and produces methane, a strong greenhouse gas. Composting avoids this and returns nutrients to the soil.

prepare: Empty the bottle or jar and give it a quick rinse.
Remove metal or plastic lids and recycle them separately.
Labels can usually stay on.
brown-glass.dispose: Place in the glass bank or glass bin. Where colours are separated, use the brown section.
avoid: Do not include ceramics, Pyrex or oven glass, mirrors, or window glass; they melt differently and spoil a batch.
brown-glass.tip: Colour sorting matters: mixing colours lowers the quality of recycled glass.
brown-glass.environment: Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality, and using recycled glass saves raw materials and furnace energy.

prepare: Flatten boxes to save space.
Remove tape, staples, and plastic inserts where possible.
Keep it dry.
cardboard.dispose: Place flattened cardboard in the paper/cardboard bin or take it to a cardboard collection point.
avoid: Do not recycle heavily greasy or food-soiled cardboard (for example pizza-box bases); tear off the clean part and bin the rest.
cardboard.tip: Wet or soiled cardboard cannot be turned back into paper pulp efficiently.
cardboard.environment: Recycling cardboard reduces the number of trees cut for new paper fibre and cuts the volume going to landfill.

clothes.bin: Clothing donation bin or textile collection point
prepare: Wash items and make sure they are dry.
Tie pairs of socks or gloves together.
clothes.dispose: Donate wearable clothes to charity or a donation bin. Worn-out textiles can go to textile recycling points where available.
avoid: Do not put clothes in the paper or plastic recycling bin.
Do not donate wet or mouldy textiles.
clothes.tip: Reusing clothing is better than recycling it. Consider swapping, reselling, or repairing first.
clothes.environment: Producing clothes takes a lot of water and energy, so extending a garment's life is one of the most effective ways to reduce its footprint.

prepare: Empty and quickly rinse the bottle or jar.
Remove lids and recycle them separately.
green-glass.dispose: Place in the glass bank or glass bin. Where colours are separated, use the green section.
avoid: Do not include ceramics, Pyrex or oven glass, mirrors, or window glass.
green-glass.tip: Green glass is often easiest to recycle into new green bottles, so keep it separate from other colours when asked to.
green-glass.environment: Recycled glass can replace a large share of raw material in new bottles and lowers the energy needed for melting.

prepare: Empty the can or tin and rinse off food.
Flattening is optional; follow local guidance.
metal.dispose: Place in the metal or mixed recycling bin. Large metal items can go to a scrap-metal collection point.
avoid: Do not put aerosol cans that still contain product, or gas canisters, into regular recycling.
Do not include paint tins with wet paint.
metal.tip: Aluminium and steel can be separated with a magnet: steel sticks, aluminium does not.
metal.environment: Recycling metals, especially aluminium, needs far less energy than producing new metal from ore, and metals can be recycled many times.

prepare: Keep paper clean and dry.
Remove plastic windows or covers where easy.
paper.dispose: Place in the paper recycling bin. Shred confidential documents first if needed.
avoid: Do not recycle paper that is greasy, wet, or heavily soiled.
Tissues, paper towels, and thermal receipts usually do not belong in paper recycling.
paper.tip: Paper fibres get shorter each time they are recycled, so it can be recycled only a limited number of times.
paper.environment: Recycling paper saves trees and reduces water and energy use compared with making paper from fresh wood pulp.

prepare: Empty the container and rinse it.
Check the recycling number (1 to 7) on the bottom.
Follow local advice about whether lids stay on.
plastic.dispose: Place in the plastic or mixed recycling bin if your area accepts that plastic type. Soft films and bags often need a separate store drop-off.
avoid: Do not put dirty or food-filled containers in recycling.
Do not bag recyclables inside plastic bags unless your local scheme asks you to.
plastic.tip: Bottles and rigid tubs (numbers 1 and 2) are the most widely accepted. Reducing single-use plastic helps more than recycling it.
plastic.environment: Plastic can persist in the environment for a very long time and break into microplastics. Recycling keeps it in use and out of waterways.

shoes.bin: Donation bin or shoe-recycling collection point
prepare: Clean off mud and tie pairs together.
Keep shoes dry.
shoes.dispose: Donate wearable pairs. Worn-out shoes can go to shoe or textile recycling schemes run by some shops and councils.
avoid: Do not put shoes in household recycling bins; mixed materials jam sorting machines.
shoes.tip: Repair (resoling, stitching) can double a shoe's useful life.
shoes.environment: Shoes combine rubber, fabric, and glue, which makes them hard to recycle, so reuse and repair have the biggest benefit.

prepare: Check whether part of the item is recyclable (for example a clean plastic or paper part).
Bag loose waste to keep bins clean.
trash.dispose: Place in the general waste bin. This is the last option once reuse and recycling are ruled out.
avoid: Do not put hazardous items such as batteries, electronics, or chemicals in general waste.
trash.tip: This category is a catch-all. If you are unsure, retake the photo or check the item's packaging for recycling symbols.
trash.environment: Residual waste usually goes to landfill or incineration, so the best approach is to reduce what ends up here.
